body:
If the parallel-queue has access to both ports, couldn't it "wait" on a port's state to be such that it can receive messages and queue something then?

I think a better description for this object (and the various things that build on it, such as workers) would be most welcome as it's somewhat messy at the moment and hard to follow.

> If the parallel-queue has access to both ports, couldn't it "wait" on a port's state to be such that it can receive messages and queue something then?

I think a problem with waiting is that this implies not handling other operations in the meantime. So if one defined one parallel queue per pair of entangled port, that could be ok. However I think in practice one parallel queue would be used for all ports, and it would be best if it wouldn't block on an operation. 

It just so happens that in Servo the "parallel-queue" is basically some sort of master event-loop for the whole browser, which should absolutely never block and handles many other things besides forwarding of messageport tasks across agent-cluster(see the [constellation](https://github.com/servo/servo/blob/31ee5fc2f567f6b5b82c5029a7c1b3008ae493ee/components/constellation/constellation.rs#L5)). 

----

By the way I forgot to define the `postMessage` operation, which would look something like:

Let's define the below as the "messageport post-message steps".

1. If the current realm is managing the entangled port(it's either not shipped, or both ports happen to have been shipped to the same realm), add task to the port-message-queue of the entangled port.
2. If not, queue the below steps on the parallel-queue:
    - switch on the state of the port:
        a. `Managed(realm)` => queue a task on the event-loop of realm, to run the "messageport post-message steps"(this includes coming back here if he port would have been shipped by the time the task runs).
        b. `TransferInProgress(Queue)` => append task to queue.
        c. `TransferCompletionInProgress(realm)` => same as a.
        d. `TransferFailed(Queue)` =>  append task to queue.
        e. `TransferRequested(realm, Queue)` =>  append task to queue.
At the conceptual level we don't need to be conservative with handing out parallel-queues though, unless there are interdependencies.

> At the conceptual level we don't need to be conservative with handing out parallel-queues though, unless there are interdependencies.

I see. My main concern would be the possibility that specifying the behavior with many parallel-queues(one per pair of entangled ports, for example), and specifying their behavior in terms of waiting, might, like the current situation, not fully reflect implementations. 

With regards to the "waiting", one other issue I have run into, is that while the paralllel-queue has access to the "transfer state" it keeps track of for both entangled port, it doesn't have direct access to the actual ports, with access instead going through the event-loop where the port happens to be transferred to. 

While the steps of the parallel queue could indeed wait for the target port to have been "transfer-received" by a realm running on a given event-loop, and then queue a task on the relevant event-loop to "complete the transfer"(essentially merge any buffered messages with the port-message-queue of the transfer-received port), that waiting cannot guarantee the port hasn't been transferred again by the time the queued task executes. So short of having the event-loop where the target-port is found block on the "transfer completion" operation(preventing tasks from running which might transfer the port again), some sort of asynchronous workflow is required, which would take into account that fact that the parallel-queue and the event-loop run in parallel, and that therefore a port is never quite fully stable when it comes to transfer.

And that is I think the problem that implementations have solved on their own, and which might be valuable to actually reflect in the standard, especially in the light of other "cross-agent-cluster" issues that have been noted(like #3691 and #4730), and which could perhaps benefit from a similar approach.
Fair, I would definitely support a more principled approach to writing this down that helps addressing cross-agent-cluster communication in general.

Ok, it might be useful to get some input from others on how they solved the below problem:

1. How do you deal with Step 7 of the [`postMessage` steps](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/#message-port-post-message-steps), "Add a task that runs the following steps to the port message queue of targetPort", when the port message queue is inside a `dataHolder`, in other words the port has been transferred, and is currently "in-flight". 
2. When you run the "transfer-receiving steps", step 3 says to "Move all the tasks that are to fire message events in dataHolder.[[PortMessageQueue]] to the port message queue of value". How do you deal with tasks that were sent while the dataHolder was "in-flight", and that were somehow dealt with as per 1 above. 
3. When you deal with the situation described under 2 above, do you take into account that the port might be transferred again in the same task in which it the transfer-receiving-steps are run? Or that might be transferred not in the current task, but a subsequent one, perhaps before having been able to "reconcile" the transferred port-message-queue with tasks dealt with under 1 above? Do you block the event-loop while doing this reconciliation? Or do you use some sort of async workflow involving some other component that deal with the tasks under the situation at 1?

----

For example, I can see from the Blink code that:

1. As part of the "transfer-steps", transferred ports are [disentangled](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/ccd149af47315e4c6f2fc45d55be1b271f39062c/third_party/blink/renderer/core/messaging/message_port.cc#L103)
2. As part of the "transfer-receiving-steps", they are [re-entangled](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/ccd149af47315e4c6f2fc45d55be1b271f39062c/third_party/blink/renderer/core/messaging/message_port.cc#L327)

and it looks like what is transferred is not an actual "port-message-queue" containing messages, but rather a handle to an IPC backend in the form of a [`MessagePortChannel`](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/ccd149af47315e4c6f2fc45d55be1b271f39062c/third_party/blink/public/common/messaging/message_port_channel.h)

While it's note-able that the spec doesn't say to do anything with entanglement in the transfer-steps, my main interest is that I assume this is done to plug the port out-of, and back into, some IPC backend. And since this backend is not the event-loop, I wonder at what point you plug the port-message-queue into the relevant event-loop. The spec says to do this when the port is enabled: "When a port's port message queue is enabled, the event loop must use it as one of its task sources. ". 

But in practice, if the port is transfer-received, then enabled in the same task, and then immediately transferred again in the same task, you might effectively already have been queuing task from some IPC-backend onto the "wrong" event-loop, since the port has been transferred again. 

So it would be interesting to know the semantics of how the IPC backend integrates in- and out of event-loops as the port is transferred(and re-transferred), without losing messages along the way.

I haven't had a chance to fully dig into other implementations, but from a quick glance Gecko seems to come with a bunch of plumbing(`MessagePortService`, `MessagePortParent/Child`) that effectively provide it with some sort of IPC backend that must in some way integrate with the relevant event-loop(s). 

It could be useful to define these operations in the spec in some way that leaves enough flexibility to implementation yet also makes it precise enough so that interoperability is not left to chance, and also so that perhaps those operations could be re-used spec-wise to solve other cross-agent-cluster/event-loop coordination issues.

Is there a concise statement of what interop problems could arise from the current spec? For example, a small code snippet that runs a single way in all browsers, but which the spec would allow to run a different way?

This issue in Chromium sheds further light on how an enabled port integrates with the event-loop, and indeed it points to a workflow not reflected in the spec. In particular, note the "The first message in a batch is still dispatched synchronously". 

I guess this initial sync workflow is perhaps the reason for the difference in behavior in the above code snippet(Servo for example has an initial async workflow, and only dispatches tasks, one per message, if it completes, meaning the port hasn't been re-transferred in the meantime). 

https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/1145692

Six years later, I ended-up using TLA+ to formalize the algorithm I had implemented in Servo in Rust for message port. 

I wrote two TLA+ specs: 

- one [coarse-grained spec](https://github.com/gterzian/formal-web/blob/e6aead75b876f98544c336766f4aff301f271ee9/tla_specs/MessagePort.tla) that assumes the port queue is always available to queue a task, which is what the standard does, and
- another [finer-grained spec](https://github.com/gterzian/formal-web/blob/e6aead75b876f98544c336766f4aff301f271ee9/tla_specs/MessagePortExtraFG.tla) that replaces this assumption with an in-parallel algorithm managing a buffer of messages for the cross-event-loop use-case(including when we don't know where the port will end-up because it is still in transfer). 
- then I defined a refinement in TLA+ that shows both can be thought of as doing the same(the finer-grained spec just uses more steps to do what the coarser-grained one does). 

More background in [this blog post](https://medium.com/@polyglot_factotum/formalizing-messageport-afbe7846578d).

I realize most people here probably don't know TLA+, but I think it's worth taking a look. 

The take-away is that you could define the algorithm using in-parallel steps and more task queuing, which would essentially do what the Servo implementation does (I remember having a quick look at the one in FF, and seeing something quite similar), and what is defined in the finer-grained TLA+ spec. 

For you consideration.
